newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Three African states await decision on ivory trade.
newsitem.headline: Three African states await decision on ivory trade.

text.p: Zimbabwe said it was making the final vital push on Wednesday to persuade a world conference on endangered species to accept its controversial proposal to resume trade in ivory.

Environment and Tourism Minister Chen Chimutengwende told Zimbabwe state television on Wednesday he was confident the 10-day Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) would grant the country its request when it votes on the issue later in the day.
But Wayne Pacelle, vice-president for government affairs of leading environmental pressure group Humane Society of the United States, urged the world forum to turn down the application.

Zimbabwe, and two other southern African states -- Botswana and Namibia -- have applied to the CITES conference ending in Harare on Friday to be exempted from a 1989 world ban on ivory trade, arguing that they have "excess" elephant herds.
On Tuesday, CITES postponed a decision on the application after a four-hour heated debate that went well past the conference closing time.

"We have not given up. We are making the final vital push and we are still very confident," Chimutengwende said, adding he was deriving his confidence from the very small margin of votes that defeated an amendment proposed by South Africa that would have eased the ban to allow commercial trade to start only in 1999, with some fixed quotas.

South Africa's proposed amendment was just three votes short of the 78 three-thirds majority it needed from the 123 countries that voted. Forty-one countries voted against the amendment, and seven abstained.

The three southern African states argue that limited and strictly supervised trade will not threaten their "excess' elephant herd, now estimated at around 150,000, and which they say is twice the land's carrying capacity.

They are strongly backed by Japan and Switzerland but face stiff opposition from influential green movements and countries, including the United States and from the European Union who argue that easing the ban will leave elephants at the mercy of poachers.
